I've written the notes below, but they're incomplete. My tool budget ran out early, after the first page reads and a few searches, so they're built only from the search-result extracts I already had. That means three gaps:

- **Verses 7–16 are thin.** Little came back on Ebed-melech, the third entrance or the oath.
- **I found nothing for part 3.** That covers Catholic and Orthodox readings, bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes and prosperity or similar modern teaching, so those are left out. Re-running searches on those sites would fill the gap.
- **Tradition labels are approximate.** The studylight.org pages tag each commentator's tradition, and I used those tags. Where several commentaries are mixed together on one biblehub.com page, I name a writer only when the extract makes clear who said it.

---

## Jeremiah 38 – Research notes

**v. 1**
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks two Pashhurs are named here. One is probably the Pashhur who put Jeremiah in the stocks (ch. 20); the other was on Zedekiah's first delegation to the prophet (ch. 21). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-38.html
- Pett notes that seals bearing the names of Gedaliah son of Pashhur and Jucal son of Shelemiah have been dug up in the City of David. https://studylight.org/commentaries/pet/jeremiah-38.html
- Tremper Longman (quoted by Precept Austin) thinks these officials were probably a pro-Egyptian party. To them Jeremiah sounded like a Babylonian agent. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-38-commentary
- G. Campbell Morgan (quoted by Guzik) says these were the politicians who had pushed the king to resist Babylon against the prophet's word. https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Jer/Jer-38.cfm

**v. 2**
- Calvin (Reformed) reads "his life as a spoil" as a hard condition. Deserters would save their lives but lose everything else, like people escaping a shipwreck. He takes the repeated "he will live" as an urgent appeal. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-2.html
- Gill explains that "goes out" means leaving the city, laying down arms and surrendering to the Chaldeans' mercy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-2.html
- Pett pictures the person seizing their life like a hunter's catch and carrying it off safely. https://studylight.org/commentaries/pet/jeremiah-38.html
- Precept Austin sees a threefold promise: they will live, keep their life as spoil, and go on living. It says the call to surrender is obedience to God's revealed will, not defeatism. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-38-commentary
- Keil & Delitzsch point out that the words are essentially the same as Jer 21:9. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/38-2.htm
- Guzik: Jeremiah was urging surrender so the people could live in exile and wait for the promised restoration. https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Jer/Jer-38.cfm
- The Bible Says calls the Chaldeans God's instruments of discipline, so resisting them defied God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/jer-38-v1-13.cfm

**v. 3**
- Matthew Henry: Jeremiah repeats that, however long the city holds out, it will be taken in the end. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-2.html
- Constable thinks Jeremiah was apparently preaching this from the court of the guard (37:21). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-2.html

**v. 4**
- Bob Utley (bible.org): "discouraging" literally means "weakening the hands." "The men of war who are left" suggests casualties and desertions. He says the officials deliberately ignored the promise of life in v. 2. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-38
- Calvin: "hands" stands for courage, so weakening them means making men too listless to move a finger. https://www.ccel.org/study/Jeremiah_38:1-13
- Keil & Delitzsch grant that the charge was possibly true: his preaching would make soldiers unwilling to fight. But it was unjust, because he spoke God's word out of love, not cowardice. The courage he undermined was "carnal obstinacy," not trust in God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/38-4.htm
- The Geneva Bible note sees the wicked who can't bear God's truth seeking to kill his ministers as lawbreakers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/38-4.htm
- Guzik says the charge was the exact opposite of the truth. He traces the same pattern with Moses, Job and Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-38/
- Precept Austin: what they called "harm" was really God's merciful warning. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-38-commentary
- A biblehub.com Q&A page links the Lachish letters' phrase "weaken our hands" to this complaint. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_didn_t_Zedekiah_oppose_officials.htm

**v. 5**
- **Spurgeon (Baptist)** preached a whole sermon on this verse, "Zedekiah; or, the Man who cannot say 'No'." His points: Zedekiah is ruled by the princes he should command, and he wants a quiet life at any price. Spurgeon says peace at any price is bought too dearly. That kind of softness ends in doing injustice to God and good men, and finally in getting no good from God's prophets. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/zedekiah-or-the-man-who-cannot-say-no
- Several writers compare Zedekiah with Pilate:
  - Derek Kidner calls it perhaps the most abject surrender in the Bible until Pilate washed his hands. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-38-commentary
  - Constable: "an early-day Pontius Pilate." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-5.html
  - Ironside: words that, like Pilate's, don't lessen his guilt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/jeremiah-38.html
- Adam Clarke (Wesleyan) calls him a "poor weak prince" who respects the prophet but fears the faction. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-5.html
- Utley compares Saul (1 Sam 15:24) and David (2 Sam 3:39), and notes the wordplay on "hand." https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-38
- **Commentators differ on what the king meant:**
  - Gill: either flattery (he could deny them nothing) or a complaint that he was "a king, and no king."
  - Poole: he means "I won't oppose you, but I won't be the author of it." Poole points to the king's later kindness to Jeremiah.
  - Keil & Delitzsch disagree. They see "inward aversion" to God's messenger and deny that the words show any wish to save him.
  - Cambridge notes that the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) makes the clause the narrator's comment.

  Source for all four: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/38-5.htm
- Calvin hears a bitter complaint from the king. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-5.html
- Benson (Methodist) quotes Blaney: the king spoke in disgust at the princes for blocking his mercy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/jeremiah-38.html
- The biblehub.com Q&A explains it through his vassal status, fragile authority, indecision and unbelief (2 Chr 36:12–13). It sees Christ as the faithful King in contrast. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_didn_t_Zedekiah_oppose_officials.htm

**v. 6**
- Guzik: lowering him with ropes was meant to kill him slowly without technically shedding blood. He compares Joseph's brothers (Gen 37). He notes that most Jerusalem houses had private cisterns. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-38/
- Ellicott (on biblehub.com) says the leaders may have shrunk from a public execution, or thought they could avoid the guilt of shedding a prophet's blood. He thinks Lam 3:53–55 probably remembers this. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/38-6.htm
- Benson thinks Jeremiah's writing all of Lamentations 3 here is "highly improbable." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/jeremiah-38.html
- Josephus, cited by Gill, Benson and Matthew Henry, says he sank up to his neck. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_038.cfm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: this was an emptied cistern, not an underground cell, and empty cisterns were often used as prisons (Zech 9:11). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/38-6.htm
- **Jeremiah as a picture of Christ:**
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls Jeremiah "a type of Messiah" (Ps 69:2). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/38-6.htm
  - Trapp: "a typical hell," and Jeremiah a type of Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/jeremiah-38.html
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says his sufferings suggest Christ's. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-38.html
- Calvin calls it hardened impiety and savage cruelty against a man who had only obeyed God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-6.html

**vv. 7–13 (Ebed-melech)** *(limited material)*
- Guzik: Ebed-melech was a foreigner, possibly a eunuch shut out of Jewish worship, yet he showed more godly compassion than the rulers. He risked his own safety. He padded the ropes so he could rescue the half-starved prophet in the safest, most comfortable way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-38/
- Matthew Henry: Ebed-melech "appears truly brave." He told the king plainly that Jeremiah had been wronged, though the princes had the king's own warrant. Henry asks where wronged innocence should go for protection but to the throne. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_038.cfm
- A biblehub.com study note sees the same ropes now used to rescue as a picture of God's reversal and mercy (Gen 50:20). https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/38-6.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary explains the Hebrew words for the rags: "shreds, tatters" and soft, worn rags. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-38.html

**v. 15**
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says the KJV question mark is an error. It should read as a statement: "Thou wilt not hearken." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-38.html

**v. 16**
- Precept Austin: Zedekiah swore by the covenant name and by God as giver of life. He was "a religious man but a weak, indecisive one." The oath is ironic, since he had broken an earlier oath to Nebuchadnezzar (2 Chr 36:13; Ezek 17). His promise is double: no harm and no betrayal. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-38-commentary
- Poole: the oath protects Jeremiah from punishment for telling the truth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/jeremiah-38.html

**vv. 17–18**
- Guzik:
  - This was not a new word, only a more urgent one.
  - The city's fate rested on one man's repentance.
  - Having surrendered to Judah's princes, Zedekiah is now told to surrender to the right princes.
  - Source: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-38/ and https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Jer/Jer-38.cfm
- Calvin: the offer of lighter punishment was no common mercy, since Zedekiah had been stubborn for years. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-17.html
- Constable: the hidden question was probably "Has the Lord changed His mind?" God hadn't, but Zedekiah needed to change his. Ironically, Babylonian officers would have spared Zedekiah while Judean officials tried to kill Jeremiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-17.html
- Gill: the "officers" were Babylon's generals (39:3); the king himself was at Riblah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-17.html
- Precept Austin reads "you will not escape" as hinting that God foresaw his attempt to flee. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-38-commentary

**v. 19**
- Barnes (Presbyterian): the deserters were probably a large party, angry that Zedekiah had rejected their advice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-19.html
- Wesley (Methodist): he feared being handed over to the Jews who had gone over to the Chaldeans. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-19.html
- Benson: he feared mockery for doing at last what he had blamed them for. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-19.html
- Pett: these fears suggest Zedekiah was actually considering surrender. https://studylight.org/commentaries/pet/jeremiah-38.html
- A. F. Muir (Pulpit homily): pride, the refusal to admit error, is one of the first hindrances to salvation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-38.html

**v. 20**
- Guzik: obeying the voice of the Lord is always the safest course. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-38/
- Precept Austin: this is the second time Zedekiah is promised his life. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-38-commentary
- D. Young (Pulpit homily): part of the harm of doubt is that while we hesitate, the chance to do good passes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-38.html

**v. 22**
- Barnes, the Pulpit Commentary and Keil & Delitzsch call it a mocking two-line song. The first line echoes Obadiah 7. The "women" are the harems of earlier kings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/38-22.htm
- **Zedekiah stuck in the mud like Jeremiah:**
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: a just repayment for Jeremiah's literal sinking. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/38-22.htm
  - Peake (quoted in Cambridge): when Zedekiah's feet sank, "no one drew him out." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/38-22.htm
  - Constable: Zedekiah would be stuck politically and spiritually as Jeremiah was physically. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-22.html
- Gill rejects a literal quagmire during his flight and takes the phrase figuratively. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-22.html
- Wesley: "Thou that art afraid of the insultings of men, shalt fall under the insultings of the women." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/jeremiah-38.html
- Matthew Henry: the women will taunt him that his "friends" have proved his real enemies. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_038.cfm

**v. 23**
- Guzik: Babylon's conquest was certain, but one man's obedience could decide how bad it would be. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-38/
- D. Young (Pulpit homily) calls it "irresolution" rather than defiance: Zedekiah kept hoping against hope. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-38.html

**vv. 24–26**
- Matthew Henry: Zedekiah has nothing to say against the advice but won't follow it. He wants secrecy for his own reputation more than for Jeremiah's safety. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-27.html
- Calvin: his fear shows he believed Jeremiah, yet chose to live in trembling. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-24.html
- Gill hears a veiled threat in "you will not die." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-24.html
- Precept Austin's heading: "Zedekiah recommends Jeremiah tell a lie." https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-38-commentary

**v. 27: a real Protestant disagreement (did Jeremiah deceive?)**
- **Reformed (Calvin):** Jeremiah reports what he did "but does not commend" it. Saying he came only to plead for his life "was not true," so the evasion can't be wholly excused. He should have followed God's call to plain dealing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-27.html
- **Baptist (Gill):** what he said was true, though not the whole truth. He wasn't obliged to say more, having no command from God and being forbidden by the king. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-27.html
- **Wesleyan/Methodist:**
  - Clarke, quoted by Precept Austin: the truth and nothing but the truth, though not the whole truth.
  - Clarke on studylight.org: Jeremiah wasn't obliged to say anything that would set the weak king against the princes or endanger his own life.
  - Benson: a person needn't reveal the whole truth to those with no right to it.
  - Source: https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-38-commentary ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-27.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/jeremiah-38.html
- **Matthew Henry:** "no lie or equivocation." We must be harmless as doves and never lie, but wise as serpents and not tell all we know. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_038.cfm
- **Restoration Movement (Coffman):** he rejects criticism of "the ethics of Jeremiah" outright. Jeremiah obeyed his king and owed the truth to no murderers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/38-27.html
- **Middle views:**
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: true, but Scripture gives no approval; "Fear drove him to it." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/38-27.htm
  - Gray: the deliberate lie is "beyond belief." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/jeremiah-38.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary notes the controversy and asks whether anyone must tell the truth to a murderer. S. Conway's homily sets out both sides: that it "comes very near to deception," and replies such as Rahab's example. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-38.html

**v. 28**
- The Pulpit Commentary: "and he was there when…" is a poor rendering. Following Coverdale, those words should begin chapter 39. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-38.html
- Precept Austin: Jeremiah is willing to be God's instrument, bearing great suffering without complaint and speaking boldly. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-38-commentary
